shared_components.rationale: lineitem (60M rows, ~4.2GB) is the largest table and touched by 17 queries. On HDD, a full sequential scan takes ~5s with parallel column reads. 11 queries benefit from consuming a single shared scan (applying residual filters per-query) rather than each performing independent scans, saving ~50s of I/O. Queries using index-based access (Q4, Q9, Q17, Q19, Q20, Q21) are excluded as their indexed paths are more efficient.
shared_components.notes: Each consumer applies its own WHERE filters (date ranges, returnflag, shipmode, etc.) as residual predicates on the shared scan stream. Zone-map-eligible queries (Q6 at 15.7%, Q14 at 1.3%, Q15 at 3.9%) accept processing extra rows in exchange for zero additional I/O.

shared_components.rationale: orders (15M rows, ~600MB) is touched by 12 queries via joins on o_orderkey (from lineitem scan) or o_custkey (from customer), or direct date-range filters. Loading orders into memory once and serving all 12 consumers saves 11 redundant HDD reads, amortizing ~22s of I/O. The dense_pk index (o_orderkey->row_id) enables O(1) lookups from in-memory arrays.
shared_components.notes: Q4 uses o_orderdate zone map filter (3.9%). Q13 uses custkey_to_orders grouped_fk. Q22 uses custkey_to_orders for NOT EXISTS check. All benefit from orders data being resident in memory.

shared_components.rationale: customer (1.5M rows, ~120MB) is joined by 7 queries via c_custkey=o_custkey and scanned by Q13/Q22. Building a shared hash once (or loading via dense_pk for O(1) lookup) avoids 7 redundant HDD reads of ~120MB each, saving ~2.8s of I/O. Different queries need different payload subsets (Q3 needs c_mktsegment, Q10 needs c_name/c_acctbal/c_phone/c_address/c_comment, Q5/Q7/Q8 need c_nationkey), so the superset of all columns is materialized.
shared_components.notes: customer has dense_pk (c_custkey->row_id) so the hash is effectively an in-memory array indexed by custkey. Q13 LEFT JOINs and Q22 scans customer directly — both benefit from the loaded data.

shared_components.rationale: part (2M rows, ~80MB) is probed by 8 queries for join filtering or predicate evaluation on part attributes (p_type, p_brand, p_container, p_size, p_name). Loading part once avoids 7 redundant HDD reads, saving ~2.1s. Queries apply diverse part filters as residuals: Q2 (p_size=15, p_type LIKE '%BRASS'), Q8 (p_type='ECONOMY ANODIZED STEEL'), Q9 (p_name LIKE '%green%'), Q14 (p_type LIKE 'PROMO%'), Q16 (p_brand<>'Brand#45', p_size IN(...)), Q17 (p_brand='Brand#23', p_container='MED BOX'), Q19 (multi-brand OR), Q20 (p_name LIKE 'forest%').
shared_components.notes: part has dense_pk so the hash is an in-memory array indexed by p_partkey. Queries using lineitem_partkey_grouped index (Q9, Q17, Q19, Q20) can filter part first, then use the index for selective lineitem access.

shared_components.rationale: partsupp (8M rows, ~192MB) is joined by 5 queries to part and/or supplier. Loading once saves 4 redundant HDD reads of ~192MB, amortizing ~2.4s. The partsupp_partkey_idx (dense_range) and partsupp_composite_hash index are available for selective lookups once data is in memory.
shared_components.notes: Q2 and Q16 join partsupp↔part. Q9 joins partsupp↔lineitem on composite key. Q11 joins partsupp↔supplier. Q20 filters via correlated subquery. The composite hash index enables O(1) (partkey,suppkey)->row_id lookups.

shared_components.rationale: supplier (100K rows, ~8MB) is the most widely shared dimension table, touched by 10 queries. Although each individual load is cheap (~30ms), 10 consumers accumulate ~270ms of savings. Multiple queries filter by nation through supplier.s_nationkey (Q2: EUROPE, Q5: ASIA, Q7: FRANCE/GERMANY, Q11: GERMANY, Q20: CANADA, Q21: SAUDI ARABIA), making the unfiltered shared load the correct superset.
shared_components.notes: supplier has dense_pk (s_suppkey->row_id, max_key=100000). Nation filtering is applied per-query as a residual via s_nationkey->nation dense_pk lookup. Q16 uses anti-join on s_comment LIKE '%Customer%Complaints%'.

rejected_candidates.reason: Q6 and Q20 share identical l_shipdate range [1994-01-01, 1995-01-01), but Q6 is already a consumer of scan_lineitem_full (full scan), and Q20 accesses lineitem via lineitem_partkey_grouped index from filtered part/partsupp. A dedicated filtered scan has only 1 effective unique consumer.

8 queries share this FK-PK join, but materializing it produces ~60M rows (same cardinality as lineitem with appended orders columns), roughly doubling memory usage. Since orders has a dense_pk index (o_orderkey->row_id) enabling O(1) lookups from the shared in-memory orders data, each query can perform the join inline at negligible CPU cost.

7 queries share this join, but each applies very different date/status filters on orders (Q3: o_orderdate < 1995-03-15, Q5: 1994 range, Q10: 1993 Q4 range, Q13: LEFT JOIN, etc.). Materializing the full 15M-row result wastes memory for queries that need only 3-5% of orders. Per-query filtered join from shared scans is more efficient.

This expression appears in Q3, Q5, Q7, Q8, Q9, Q10, Q14, Q19, but each query groups by different keys (l_orderkey, n_name, nation pairs, o_year, c_custkey, none) and applies different WHERE filters, making a shared partial aggregation impossible without producing a cross-product of all group-by dimensions.

orders has a dense_pk index (o_orderkey->row_id, max_key=60000000) providing O(1) array-based lookup. A hash table on o_orderkey would be redundant and use ~240MB vs the existing index. scan_orders_full already loads orders data into memory.

6 queries (Q2, Q5, Q9, Q11, Q20, Q21) join supplier to nation, but nation has only 25 rows and a dense_pk index. The join is a single array lookup per supplier row (~0.1ms total), making a shared materialized join unprofitable — accounting overhead exceeds the <1ms computation saved.

Q7 and Q14 could share a superset scan for l_shipdate [1995-01-01, 1996-12-31]. However, Q14's filter (1995-09-01 to 1995-10-01, 1.3% selectivity) benefits enormously from zone map skipping on HDD. Both queries are already consumers of scan_lineitem_full, making a dedicated filtered scan redundant.
